The canvas, the sizes, the sections and the hero for every theme build; a custom run designs its own (`direction.md`). A page looks made when every screen holds one idea at the right size. Numbers are at 1440 x 900 unless a line says otherwise.

## 1. The canvas

- **One container, centred and capped:** `.container` from the scaffold, `--container` 1440px with `--gutter` 64px, so content is 1312px wide at 1440 and stays 1312px at 1920 while the gutters grow (44d).
- **Twelve columns inside it**, `--gap-columns` 32px apart: one column is 80px, four 416px, six 640px, eight 864px. Every section places its parts on these columns, so left edges line up from the nav to the footer.
- **Every section:** the outer element owns the background and the block padding, the inner `.container` the width and only `padding-inline` (a `padding` shorthand there silently zeroes the rhythm). A full-bleed band changes the background and keeps the container.

## 2. Sizes

The scaffold writes these tokens and `base.css` sets them on the elements. A theme changes faces, weights, tracking and case; the steps hold, except where a theme sets its display a step larger.

| Role | Token | At 1440 | Element |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hero head | `--text-display` | 84px | `h1` |
| Long hero head, statement | `--text-display-s` | 60px | `.display-s` |
| Section head | `--text-section` | 52px | `h2` |
| Item title | `--text-title` | 25px | `h3` |
| Lead (the one line under a head) | `--text-lead` | 21px | `.lead` |
| Body | `--text-md` | 16px | `p` |
| Label, caption, meta | `--text-sm` | 14px | `small`, `figcaption`, `th` |

- A section head under 40px at 1440 is the most common reason a page looks unfinished (78). The hero head is about one and a half times the section head, the section head about twice the item title.
- A head and its line sit 16 to 24px apart (`--space-md` to `--space-lg`); the head block and the section's content 48 to 64px (`--space-2xl`), 40px in a tight composition.
- Grid items sit `--gap-columns` apart across and 48 to 64px apart down; a card or well takes 32 to 40px of padding.

## 3. Rhythm between sections

- Sections part by the three scaffold steps, `--section-gap-s` 120px, `--section-gap` 144px and `--section-gap-l` 176px, mixed (59). A band (a change of paper) takes `--section-gap-s` of padding top and bottom.
- Space is earned by mass: a 144px gap frames a 700px section and is a hole under a 200px one. An empty-looking page wants a bigger head, a bigger visual or a fuller section, not a smaller gap.
- Six to nine sections, hero and footer included; five on a thin prompt, never fewer. Height follows content (often 5,000 to 8,000px with pictures and a full prompt, 3,000 to 4,000px on a thin one); never pad toward a height.

## 4. A section

A section is one piece of the page's content shown at its best: the menu, the lineup, the latest issue, the product at work, the room, the price. Decide the content first, then the composition that shows it best. Most sections carry a **head block** above or beside a **body** from § 5; a section whose content names itself (a menu, a timetable, a track list, a list of issues, the product's own screen) may go without one, or carry its head inside the content (the menu's own title, the date over the lineup). Never more than two neighbours with the same skeleton: a page of head-then-block, head-then-block reads as a template however good each block is. What real sites in each category are built around is in `anatomy.md`.

- **The head block:** an `h2` of six words or fewer at `--text-section` (a staged shape may head each stage with its one-word name), at most one line at `--text-lead` beneath it, on columns 1 to 6 or 1 to 7, or split (head on 1 to 5, the line on 7 to 12, baselines aligned). Centred only over a symmetric body, and never more centred head blocks than left-aligned ones.
- **The body fills the width:** its widest row reaches ten of the twelve columns (77). A narrow text block with the right half empty is the sparse page's signature; pair it with a visual, split it, or set it as a statement.
- **The body has mass:** a visual 360px tall or more; a set of three or four items across the width; a list or table of three or more rows across ten columns; a working control on the prompt's own facts; or a statement at `--text-section` or larger. A head and a paragraph are a head block, never a section.
- **A split balances:** text and visual centre on each other within 60px, and neither column leaves more than a fifth of the row empty.
- **Content sets the height:** usually 520 to 900px; under 360px only for a band (a call to action, a logo row, a statement), at most twice a page.

## 5. Compositions

Layouts, not components: build each in the theme's material and the prompt's content. A page uses three to six different ones and never the same one twice in a row, except in a one-composition shape (Split Studio, Feature Stack, Catalogue), where neighbours change ratio and, where the shape allows, side.

1. **Split.** A text block (head, line, two to four short facts or one action) beside a visual on columns 6 to 12 or 7 to 12, 440px tall or more at 4:3 to 4:5 (portrait for a product photograph). Swap the side at most once a page; change the ratio (5 and 7, 4 and 8, 6 and 6) between two splits.
2. **Showcase.** The head block, then one visual across all twelve columns at 16:9 to 21:9, 560px tall or more; beneath it at most two smaller visuals at 8 and 4 or 7 and 5, never three equal frames.
3. **Grid.** Three or four items across (or two by two): plans, products, places, rooms, dishes, each with its photograph, a large figure or a title big enough to carry the cell, then one line; equal heights, aligned tops, 240px or taller. Never empty frames (68), stock faces for people (F9) or icon tiles over headings (3).
4. **Bento.** Four to six tiles on six or twelve columns in mixed spans (8 and 4 over 4, 4 and 4; or 7 and 5 over 5 and 7), rows 280 to 360px, two tiles at least with a visual, one clearly the lead.
5. **Rows.** Three to five full-width rows parted by hairlines, 72 to 120px each: a title at `--text-title` on columns 1 to 5, its line or figure on 6 to 12. A head block may sit on 1 to 4 beside rows on 5 to 12 (an FAQ, an index, a timeline, a price list).
6. **Table.** Full width, four or five rows of 56 to 72px, numerals tabular, the column that names the row one step heavier.
7. **Figures.** Three or four real numbers at `--text-display-s`, labels beneath, across the twelve columns, parted by vertical hairlines. Only figures the user gave (46a).
8. **Steps.** Three or four stages across, each a numeral (a real `<ol>`, never a `01` label over a head, 54), a title and a line, with a visual beneath or beside where the material has one; or a vertical run with a visual per stage on a fixed side.
9. **Statement.** One sentence filling eight to ten columns in two or three lines, from `--text-section` up to `--text-display` (a condensed or light face takes the larger step), with its attribution or one action; once a page.
10. **Band.** A change of paper (`--color-paper-2`, the ink, or a field of the accent where the posture allows) edge to edge, the container inside, holding whatever the page's job wants there: the next free table times, the buy box, the store buttons beside a screen, the next date and the address. Never an email field by default (85).
11. **Form.** The fields on six or seven columns beside the head block and two to four facts, inputs 48 to 56px tall, one primary action.
12. **Rail.** A horizontal run past the container's edge (dates, issues, products, rooms, episodes), five or more items with the next one cut by the edge, scrollable by touch and keyboard, snap points, no arrows needed past two.
13. **Pinned.** One visual held sticky on six or seven columns while three or four short panels scroll past it on the other side, each changing what the visual shows (a state, a crop, a step); static under 60rem.
14. **Switcher.** One area with two to five states behind a segmented control: the menu by lunch and dinner, the plans by month and year, the app on phone and watch, the schedule by day. Every state real; the first visible without script.
15. **Index.** A dense, scannable list of the prompt's own items with their facts in columns (issues with dates and topics, projects with year and client, episodes with length, lots with estimates), optionally filtered; 6 to 20 rows, the lead row larger.
16. **Schedule.** Time against place or day: a two-day festival as two columns of acts and times, a week of classes, opening hours as a strip; the current or next slot marked. Only for times the visitor picks or plans around, never a process, a workday or a delivery told as clock times.
17. **Offer.** The thing for sale with what a buyer needs at the moment of buying: the photograph or screen, the options (size, scent, plan), the price, the action and one line of delivery or terms. On a buy page it is often the hero.

Under 60rem every composition stacks in reading order: the head block, then the body; a split's visual after its text; a grid two across, then one under 40rem; a bento's lead tile first; a rail stays a rail; a pinned pair unpins; a schedule turns into one column per day. Visuals keep their aspect ratio and lose their minimum height; nothing scrolls sideways except a rail or a table that says so (`responsive.md`).

## 6. The hero

The first screen at 1440 x 900 and 1920 x 1080, and only the first screen (44c). Pick a posture at Step 2 from the job (`anatomy.md`), stamp it, and vary it run to run; text beside a picture (Settled, Stage) is the most common generated hero, so take it only when the picture is the strongest thing the prompt has.

| Posture | Height | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Settled** | fills the screen under the nav | centred in the screen; the text on six columns, the visual on the other six |
| **Stage** | fills the screen under the nav | the text on five columns, a visual on seven at 60 to 75% of the screen tall (reversed when a poster-size head needs the width); it may bleed off the outer edge |
| **Banner** | 50 to 60% of the screen | the first section shows above the fold; for references, docs, utilities |
| **Ledge** | fills the screen | a tall field above, the head resting at the base; at 1920 the head grows to its cap first |
| **Corridor** | fills the screen | one centred column of 44ch or less, the head larger than usual |
| **Poster** | 92 to 100dvh | a full-bleed photograph or canvas, the content on its calmest part with room around it, low and left or centred, never squeezed into a corner |
| **Counter** | fills the screen under the nav | the action is the visual: the subscribe field with the latest issue, the booking times, the buy box with its options, the download with the screen, set large beside or under a shorter head |
| **Index** | fills the screen under the nav | the content is the visual: the lineup, the menu, the list of issues or projects, set as the page's lead with the head small above it; for pages whose list is the reason to come |

- **Centred in its screen.** For Settled, Stage, Banner and Corridor the space under the content is 1.0 to 1.5 times the space above it (44a), and the lowest content sits within 160px of the fold (79). Spend spare height on a larger visual or larger type, never on copy.
- **The visual is big:** six or seven columns wide and 60% of the screen tall or more (520px at 1440 x 900), or a portrait object (a cover, a phone, a bottle) at 75% tall on four or five columns; its centre within 60px of the text block's. The hero grid is two tracks (`6fr 5fr`, `5fr 7fr`) with its own gap of `--space-2xl` to `--space-3xl`, so text and visual stand 48 to 120px apart; spans on the twelve columns leave an empty column between them. Under 60rem the gap becomes a row gap of `--space-xl`. What it shows is `imagery.md` § 1; a working form is a section or a close, not the default hero.
- **No visual:** the head grows to `--text-display` at its cap across eight to twelve columns, or the posture is Banner and the first section starts by 640px.
- **The text:** the head (seven words or fewer), one sentence at `--text-lead`, one or two actions (58). Under 60rem every posture collapses to its content's height (Poster may stay full-bleed).

## 7. The page

- **The job decides the anatomy** (`anatomy.md`): where the action lives (in the hero, sticky, repeated beside the content, at the close), and which category-native sections the page is built around. A newsletter puts the subscribe field in the hero and shows the issues; a restaurant shows the menu and the booking; a band shows the record and the dates. The theme dresses that anatomy; it never replaces it.
- **Order follows the argument the shape makes** (`macrostructures.md`), never hero, three features, a call to action and a footer (8). Lead with the strongest real thing after the hero; put each fact where it does work.
- **Not every page has steps, figures or a schedule.** Steps only for a process the visitor really goes through (booking, joining, getting a festival ticket); a figure row only for three numbers the prompt states outright, never one derived from it (365 mornings from "every day"). Together they appear on most generated pages; on a made page they are a choice.
- **Variety:** never the same composition in neighbouring sections (a one-composition shape aside); mirror a split once at most, never a zigzag; one full-width visual at least on a product page; one or two bands. Read the log's `sections`: a Statement, Steps, Figures and a closing Band are the easiest reaches, so when the last build used one, make that beat another way.
- **Balance:** photographs take a quarter to a third of the page below the hero (83), and never lead two sections in a row; the sections between are built from the theme's material (its Range: type, figures, rules, the product, a table, a form). `imagery.md` § 5 has the counts.
- **Pace:** a dense section (a grid, a table, a bento, an index) is followed by a quiet one (a statement, a showcase); the page ends on a real close.
- **The close is the job, not a form.** End on what the visitor came to do, in the form the job takes (the next times to book, the buy box, the store buttons, the next date and the address, the latest issue), or simply on the last strong section and the footer. An email field closes a page only when the job is one where a mailing list is native (subscribe, join, attend, listen, visit) and the anatomy calls for it, or the user asked for one (85); a page whose action already sits in the hero or a sticky bar need not repeat it at the foot.
- **The footer closes the page:** 200 to 400px: the wordmark or one closing line, the page's real links, the legal line. A single line under a hairline is a colophon, right for a letter, a document or a manifesto.
- **The nav is one line, 56 to 80px tall**, sized to the page's real destinations. Vary it against the log: edge-aligned (wordmark and one or two links or an action at opposite edges), a floating pill, a masthead (a large centred wordmark over a rule), a slab (a heavy full-width bar), a search-led bar with a visible command pill, a banner over a bar that retracts on scroll, a three-part bar only for four or more real destinations (42). A side rail only where a sticky object earns it.
- **Footers:** a mast (the wordmark large over the links), a statement (one closing sentence large, the links beneath), a colophon block (credits and address as one paragraph), newsletter-first (the form leads; only for a subscribe page), a letter close (a sign-off and a date), index columns only for a hub with a real sitemap.

## 8. Before shipping

Scroll the page at 1440 x 900 one screen at a time: is something on each screen big enough to be its reason? A screen holding only a heading and a line wants a bigger visual, the line set as a statement, or two sections merged. Then squint: with the words blurred, each section still has a shape and the page a rhythm of heavy and light. The render tier measures width (77), head scale (78), the hero's foot (79) and the photo share (83); the eye judges the rest.

## 01 · Bento Grid

Modular blocks of varying sizes laid out as an irregular grid. Each block is a feature, a figure the user gave, an image or a supplied quote. Rhythm comes from size variation, not card uniformity.

- **Heading:** a display head over the grid's first row; the hero is one screen and the grid starts inside it or right under it (44c), never a tall empty band.
- **Body:** asymmetric grid, six to nine blocks of mixed spans (1×1, 2×1, 1×2, 2×2); image-bearing tracks `minmax(0, 1fr)` (50).
- **Divider:** one gap, `--gap-columns`; no rules; the grid is the rhythm.
- **Button:** an outlined chip in the hero; inside a tile, a typographic link carrying a verb.
- **Image:** tightly cropped inside individual blocks; never full-bleed.
- **Reveal:** none, or one one-shot fade as the grid enters.

Reach for it when the prompt is "many small things to show": a feature page, a SaaS landing, anywhere visitors have several equally valid entry points. A block holding a figure or a quote exists only when the user supplied it (46a).

Avoid when the message is one hero idea. Bento spreads attention; a one-idea page wants Marquee or Stat-Led.

Compositions: Bento and Grid (`layout.md` § 5).

**Sample opening lines** (imitate the specificity, not the wording):
> *"Distributed tracing that explains itself."* Names the category and the promise in five words (Tracejam).
> *"An API for sending mail from code."* Names the product class and the reader.
> *"Everything a small kitchen needs to sell online."* Names the scale and the job.

## 02 · Long Document Reads like a memo, a letter or a journal entry. No marketing structure. Continuous prose with inline section heads. The page is literature about the product. - **Heading:** inline with the body; section heads emerge from the paragraph flow as short bold phrases. - **Body:** single column, line-height 1.65 or more, measure 60 to 65ch. - **Divider:** negative space; the gap is the divider; at most one centred ornament for emphasis. - **Button:** a typographic link inside a paragraph, carrying a verb, never a separate block. It is the fold's one visible action (44b). - **Image:** inline, sized to the measure; never full-bleed. - **Reveal:** none. The page is simply there. Reach for it for case studies, founder posts, mission pages, products whose sale is philosophical. The prompt says "tell a story", not "list features". Avoid when there is one decisive action to take. Long Document hides its actions inside sentences, which is wrong for a transactional page. Heading: the inline lead-in of [`../craft.md`](../craft.md) § 7, item 3. ```html

…

A small heading.

… See the prices …

``` ```css .prose { max-width: 65ch; } .prose h2.inline { display: inline; font: inherit; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: normal; } .prose h2.inline + p { display: inline; } ``` **Sample opening lines** (imitate the specificity, not the wording): > *"Saturday, 6:14 a.m. The dough went in at midnight."* Opens on a time-stamp; the brand introduces itself as a moment in the day (Maple Street Bread). > *"A monthly publication for people who still read to the end."* Names the cadence and the reader. > *"We build one thing, and we have built it for nine years."* A verb, a count, no claim.

## 03 · Marquee Hero

The hero is the page above the fold. A single statement or visual fills the viewport. Below the fold the page becomes something else (a list, a grid, prose).

- **Heading:** display fills the fold at `clamp(4rem, 10vw, 9rem)` (`craft.md` § 1), hugging the container's edges; an uppercase head that can wrap keeps `line-height` 1.0 or more (55a).
- **Body:** below the fold, a list of work or one content block; the hero does not continue.
- **Divider:** a thick rule between hero and below-fold, or a hard change of paper.
- **Button:** one action in the fold under the statement, with the one sentence (Floor 12, 13): a typographic link or a single button. The statement owns the screen; the action and the sentence sit small at its foot.
- **Image:** none in the fold (typography is the visual), or a single full-bleed photograph as the fold's background.
- **Reveal:** the fold is static; below-fold may sweep in horizontally.

Reach for it when the brand or the person is the message: designer and director portfolios, indie products with one declarative voice, any "this is who we are" page.

Avoid for products whose value needs explaining in seconds. Marquee makes the visitor scroll before they understand.

Compositions: a Poster or Corridor hero (`layout.md` § 6); below it, Rows, Grid or a Showcase (§ 5).

**Sample opening lines** (imitate the specificity, not the wording):
> *"Type, set with care."* Three words, refusal of the verb, treats type as material.
> *"A studio for what comes next."* Names the practice without explaining it.
> *"Print discipline, on screen."* Two phrases, a promise about method.

## 04 · Stat-Led

The hero is a figure the user gave, with the line that says what it means. Everything that follows supports or qualifies it. Data is the narrative.

- **Heading:** a large numeric display at graphic scale (`craft.md` § 7, tabular figures) paired with a worded headline. The figure is the biggest element and never the hero's only words: say what it means beside or beneath it as a real headline, not a small label. Read them together: *"Four seconds. From the alert link to the slow span."*
- **Body:** sections each anchored by a supporting figure or chart.
- **Divider:** hairline rules between figure blocks; `tabular-nums` everywhere.
- **Button:** an outlined chip beneath the qualifier, labelled with a verb ("Read the report").
- **Image:** charts and data-viz per [`../data-viz.md`](../data-viz.md); product photographs only in the slots the user asked for.
- **Reveal:** number-tick on the hero figure, from 0 to the target over `--dur-long`, legal only because the figure is real; the markup holds the final figure, so it reads with scripting off and under reduced motion (62).

Reach for it when the prompt says "we have proof in numbers": enterprise and B2B, fundraising, climate and impact pages.

Avoid when the user has not given a number. Every figure on this page is the user's, with its unit and its source (46a); a bare figure with no worded line fails 46b. A fake big number is worse than no number.

Compositions: Figures for the supporting row, Rows for the qualifiers (`layout.md` § 5).

**Sample opening lines** (the number is the user's; imitate how the words complete it):
> *"Four seconds. From the alert link to the slow span."* The figure, then what it bought (Tracejam).
> *"[the user's count] posts. New CSS you could use today."* A count grounds the page in real volume.
> *"[the user's rate] faster, so the team can decide late."* A rate, then the behaviour it allows.

## 05 · Workbench

Real product captures are the primary content. The page is a guided tour of the app in use, with short captions in place of marketing copy.

- **Heading:** plain and functional at the section size; the captures do the talking.
- **Body:** a sequence of capture blocks, each a `<figure>` with a `<figcaption>` that states a fact and one inline annotation.
- **Divider:** the figure is the divider; sections separate by gap and figure.
- **Button:** the hero's one action (44b), then, where the theme allows a sticky element, a bottom bar carrying it after the third capture, labelled with the verb ("Start a project").
- **Image:** the real capture, unframed, in a `<figure>`; until the user supplies it, the product built in a `data-slot` (`imagery.md` § 4). No browser or device chrome (47a, 47b).
- **Reveal:** one type-unmask, on the first caption; the captures load instantly and the rest is simply there.

Reach for it for SaaS, developer tools, editor extensions, anywhere seeing the product in use is the sale.

Avoid when the product is conceptual or services-led. Workbench needs a UI to show.

Compositions: Showcase and Split for the captures, a Band for the close (`layout.md` § 5); the optional bar is a sticky bottom bar with one action at `--z-sticky`.

**Sample opening lines** (imitate the specificity; the page walks the visitor through):
> *"$ streampipe parse access.log --filter status=5xx | jq"* Opens on a real command, not a claim.
> *"Read anything that emits lines: files, pipes, sockets, kubectl logs."* Names the inputs, refuses abstraction.
> *"Open the trace, find the span, fix the regression."* Three concrete verbs.

## 06 · Conversational FAQ Bold questions, prompt answers. The page reads like an honest interview with the product. Each pair may be a disclosure. - **Heading:** each section is a question: a short direct phrase ending in `?`. - **Body:** the answer in one or two short paragraphs directly under the question. - **Divider:** a hairline between pairs, or no rule and a change of paper. - **Button:** a typographic link inside an answer, carrying a verb ("Read the policy"); one outlined CTA at the foot. - **Image:** sparse; at most one diagram per long answer. - **Reveal:** none on load; a disclosure opens over `--dur-long` with `--ease-out` on `grid-template-rows` from `0fr` to `1fr`. Reach for it near pricing, for products that meet scepticism, for regulated or educational fields. As the primary page it opens with a hero that asks the first question; otherwise it pairs with another shape that opens the page. ```html

How long does setup take?

…

``` **Sample opening lines** (questions are real questions; answers are short and concrete): > *"What is this for? A single-binary CLI for parsing log streams from stdin."* Names the form factor and the input (Streampipe). > *"How is it different? It runs where the logs are, so nothing leaves the box."* Answers with a fact, not a comparison. > *"Who built this? Three of us, in Lisbon, since 2014."* Date, place and count; no marketing.

## 07 · Manifesto Polemical large type. The page tells the reader what to believe before it tells them what to buy. Often a poster's posture. - **Heading:** uppercase display, tilted slightly (`-2deg` to `-4deg`) or set straight; one weight and one colour throughout, stress from a line break, never from a coloured or italic word (38i, 38iii); `line-height` 1.0 or more when it can wrap (55a). A theme whose signature is an accented word stamps the 38iii waiver and places it once, in the hero. - **Body:** short paragraphs, each one assertion, large enough to read across the room. - **Divider:** changes of paper between sections, or the theme's own rules; never a card. - **Button:** one solid block in the accent; the fold carries it beside or under the declaration (44b), and it returns at the foot as the page's last word. - **Image:** none when the cause is an idea; when it is physical (repair, housing, a river), photographs of it in the theme's treatment, one a screen at most. - **Reveal:** one horizontal sweep, on the first claim below the fold; the rest is simply there. Reach for it for repositioning announcements, mission-led indie products, a studio's beliefs page. Avoid for checkout, pricing or a product tour. Manifesto sells agreement; a call to show up, sign or join is its one action. ```html

We believe
design is slow.

It costs less than the rework you will do without it.

``` **Sample opening lines** (manifestos commit; they do not hedge): > *"We are a studio. We are not a platform."* Defines by refusal, one colour (Meridian). > *"We design products that last twelve years. We do not design products that need replacing every two."* A concrete number, a paired declaration. > *"Lightness above weight."* A one-line principle, no explanation.

## 08 · Photographic

Huge photographs lead the page. Text is small annotation, not headline. The design says look before it says read.

- **Heading:** small: the headline and its one sentence sit on a paper plate at the image's base, and a caption near a corner carries a fact in the body face; never a centred display.
- **Body:** full-bleed photograph bands alternating with sections the theme's material carries alone (its Range: a menu as rows, the hours as a table, a statement), so photographs cover up to about 45% of the page below the hero and never lead two sections in a row (83).
- **Divider:** the image edge is the divider; no rules.
- **Button:** a typographic link on the plate, under the sentence, carrying a verb; it is the fold's one visible action (44b).
- **Image:** the whole point: full-bleed, edge to edge, from the user; library photographs in slots until theirs arrive (`imagery.md` § 2).
- **Reveal:** no spatial motion; the photographs do the work.

Reach for it for fashion, hospitality, photography portfolios, lifestyle commerce, any brand whose product is a feeling.

Avoid when the subject has nothing to photograph.

Compositions: the Poster hero (`layout.md` § 6) and full-bleed Showcases (§ 5).

**Sample opening lines** (captions are dates, places and plate numbers, not marketing):
> *"Plate 47, scored before the proof."* A number and a moment in the process (Maple Street Bread).
> *"Spring, 2026."* Two words, full stop.
> *"From the working archive."* Gives the photograph provenance without explaining it.

## 09 · Quote-Led

The hero is a quote the user supplied, with its attribution. The headline is someone else's voice.

- **Heading:** italic display setting the quote at `--text-display-s`, attribution below in the body face, one quiet line. The italic is the whole head, declared on the display (38ii guard), never one word.
- **Body:** more supplied quotes, case studies or a quiet feature list.
- **Divider:** a centred quote-mark glyph or a short rule between quotes.
- **Button:** a typographic link beneath the attribution, carrying a verb ("Read the case study").
- **Image:** the real person's photograph or the company's mark beside the attribution, or nothing.
- **Reveal:** none in the fold; below the fold may stagger.

Reach for it for B2B products with strong customer voices, agency case-study pages, fundraising sites, anywhere "people like me use this" is the unlock.

Avoid when the user has not supplied the quote. The quote is the user's, verbatim, with the name, role and company as given, or the shape does not ship (46a). Never write one, never paraphrase one.

Compositions: the quote as a Statement (`layout.md` § 5), its attribution beneath; further quotes the user gave as Rows.

**Sample opening lines** (fixture quotes; on a build only the user's words go here):
> *"I started listening on a long bus ride. By the third episode I had missed my stop, and I did not mind."* Story-shaped, attributed to a listener (Tide).
> *"Restraint, repeated, becomes a signature."* Short and philosophical, signed by the studio.
> A supplied outcome quote works the same way: the customer's own sentence, the number theirs, the attribution as given.

## 10 · Specimen

Large serif display, asymmetric column spans, hairline rules, a typographic CTA, generous whitespace. The voice of a foundry, a journal or a press.

- **Heading:** a large serif phrase, standing alone. When the run is genuinely ordinal the figure is generated on the heading itself (`<ol>` with `counter()`); a number typed beside or above it is an eyebrow (54).
- **Body:** asymmetric spans: a narrow marginalia column (captions, dates, sidenotes) beside a wide content column.
- **Divider:** hairline rules between sections.
- **Button:** a typographic link carrying a verb ("Open your studio"); no box, no fill, no arrow (63).
- **Image:** none, or one photograph of the face in print (a poster, a sign, a book spread) from the library or the user.
- **Reveal:** fade-up stagger on first load.

Reach for it when the prompt is about type, publishing or writing (a foundry, a journal, a press, a specimen sheet), or the user names it; the editorial genre alone does not qualify. On any other prompt pick another shape: this is the field's most-copied look, and a vague prompt that lands here has not been read.

Avoid for product pages that need a demo; Specimen has nowhere to put one.

Compositions: Rows and a Statement (`layout.md` § 5); the action is a typographic link.

**Sample opening lines** (foundry voice, treating type as material culture):
> *"A quiet instrument."* Refusal of the verb.
> *"Type, set with care."* Three words.
> *"Set by hand, since 2003."* Date-anchored, names the method.

## 11 · Catalogue

Uniform grid of variations of the same thing: typefaces, palettes, SKUs. The page is a visual index of inventory.

- **Heading:** one line at the theme's display scale over the grid; the products lead, so the heading never pushes the first row below the fold.
- **Body:** a grid of same-sized cards, 3 to 5 per row, each one variant of the core product; image tracks `minmax(0, 1fr)` (50).
- **Divider:** hairline rules between rows.
- **Button:** a link inside each card to its detail page; no global CTA. The fold's one visible action is the first card's link (44b).
- **Image:** a specimen thumbnail or a swatch per card when the user gave the images; otherwise a library photograph of the kind of thing, or each card set in type (the name, the one fact, the price, a colour swatch where colour is the variant), never a row of empty frames (68).
- **Reveal:** none.

Reach for it for foundries, palette tools, font shops, colour systems, capsule collections.

Avoid for narrative brands. Catalogue treats every item as equal, wrong for a product with hierarchy.

Compositions: Grid (`layout.md` § 5), one card per item: its image, name, price and one action.

**Sample opening lines** (inventory headers: dated, with a count):
> *"Today's loaves."* Two words, ownership of the day (Maple Street Bread).
> *"Five collections, in store now."* The count and the where.
> *"Thirty-eight pieces this spring, every one hand-stitched."* Count, season, qualifier; no adjectives.

## 12 · Letter

First-person, written, intimate. Opens with a greeting. Reads as a personal note from the founder.

- **Heading:** the salutation in the display italic ("Dear reader,"), 1.5 to 2 times body size; the whole line one style.
- **Body:** prose, single column, narrow measure (50ch), as if typed.
- **Divider:** paragraph spacing only; an occasional `* * *` separator.
- **Button:** no button. The sign-off link at the foot carries a verb ("Join the list"). In the fold the one visible action is the link in the first paragraph (44b).
- **Image:** one signature scan, or a quiet inline photograph, or nothing.
- **Reveal:** none.

Reach for it for personal brands, indie founder announcements, sabbatical or pivot pages, donation appeals.

Avoid for transactional commerce. Letter is intimate; commerce is functional.

Compositions: the Corridor hero (`layout.md` § 6); the footer is a letter close (§ 7).

**Sample opening lines** (first-person greetings, dated, with a place if it matters):
> *"Hello, I'm Anya."* One line: a name, a full stop.
> *"Saturday, 6:14 a.m. The dough went in at midnight."* Opens on a moment, then explains it (Maple Street Bread).
> *"Hey there. This page is soft because the surface should be soft."* A colloquial open and a principle.

## 13 · Index-First

The page is a list of links. No hero image, no narrative flow. Navigation as design.

- **Heading:** a short head at the hero size naming the index (*Everything published here, newest first*) and one line; the index starts on the first screen.
- **Body:** a vertical list of categorised links; a filter row above it or a disclosure, never a sidebar by default.
- **Divider:** hairline rules between rows, or no rules and bands of paper.
- **Button:** the links are the buttons.
- **Image:** none, or one photograph of the collection itself, and a small mark by each entry.
- **Reveal:** none.

Reach for it for documentation hubs, knowledge bases, archive front pages, design-system entries, link pages with substance.

Avoid for a hard sell (a launch, a checkout). Index-First serves a browsing audience; a personal site that offers its owner's time is fine.

Compositions: Rows at full width (`layout.md` § 5).

**Sample opening lines** (headers for what sits below, sometimes no more than a line):
> *"Selected work, 2018 to 2026."* A date range, no preamble.
> *"Everything published here, newest first."* Names the sort and the scope.
> *"Writer and photographer."* Three words that summarise the whole site.

## 14 · Narrative Workflow Numbered stages tell the story of how the user uses the product over time. Each section is a phase; the page is a process timeline. - **Heading:** the stage number rides inside the heading (`

1.0 Intake

`) or is generated by `
    ` with `counter()`. Never a separate label beside the heading: that is an eyebrow at stage scale (54). - **Body:** each stage has a short explanation and one object at full size: a product capture 360px tall or more when the user gave screens, otherwise a figure or rows from the prompt (a timer, a count, the thing the stage makes). Three stages holding the same kind of object read as three features (8): vary the object from stage to stage. - **Divider:** a rule between stages, in the theme's rule weight; the number stays in the heading, never on the rule. - **Button:** the hero's one action (44b), returning once at the foot ("Start at stage one"); links inside stages. - **Image:** a real capture per stage, often annotated, in a `

## 15 · Split Studio

Diptych. Every major block divides the screen, text on one side, proof on the other, and the proof keeps its side down the page (one mirror at most, never a zigzag, `layout.md` § 7).

- **Heading:** half the screen wide; the other half holds a capture or a supplied quote.
- **Body:** text-and-proof rows that vary by weight, not by side: one lead row gives the proof the larger share, the rest split evenly; one column gap for all of them (F15).
- **Divider:** a clear gutter between halves; no rules.
- **Button:** an outlined chip below the text half.
- **Image:** on the proof side in every row: a real capture, or the product built in a slot (`imagery.md` § 4).
- **Reveal:** the hero's two halves fade in once, 60 to 100ms apart; the rows below are simply there.

Reach for it for SaaS feature pages, developer tools that pair explanation with code, anything where every claim wants a visual proof.

Avoid for narrative or photographic brands. Split halves the attention; some pages need one focus.

Compositions: Split (`layout.md` § 5), the proof keeping its side.

**Sample opening lines** (a positioning statement paired with a proof column):
> *"A studio for what comes next."* Italic display beside a selected-work column.
> *"Print discipline, on screen."* Two phrases, set like a masthead.
> *"We design and build products for small ambitious teams."* Names the verbs and the audience.

## 16 · Feature Stack

Sticky left pane holding the heading, scroll-synced right pane cycling through related captures. Paced like film.

- **Heading:** held inside the sticky pane; persists while content cycles beside it.
- **Body:** two columns, left sticky, right scrolling; the right pane plays through 3 to 6 detail captures per section.
- **Divider:** section bands; the sticky pane re-anchors per section, at `top: var(--banner-height)` under a sticky nav (56).
- **Button:** in the sticky pane, shown once the section's last capture is reached; with scripting off it is simply there (62).
- **Image:** the scrolling column is real captures, or the product built in slots until they arrive (`imagery.md` § 4); never a run of empty frames (68).
- **Reveal:** none of the fade kind; the sticky scroll is the motion. Choreograph it with [`../scroll-choreography.md`](../scroll-choreography.md) § 4 Sticky diptych with the pane kept on the left, or § 1 Pinned chapter: one pattern per page.

Reach for it for premium products, complex feature stories, anywhere the pacing should be controlled as the visitor scrolls.

Avoid for mobile-first audiences without a strong fallback. Sticky scroll-sync is rough on small screens.

Compositions: a pinned Split (`layout.md` § 5), the pin per `scroll-choreography.md` § 4.

Mobile: under 60rem the sticky pane becomes a heading above its captures, stacked in flow.

**Sample opening lines** (pin one statement, then walk the visitor through):
> *"Plan, build, ship."* Three verbs, three sticky panes.
> *"Read anything that emits lines."* Names what is possible, then walks through it (Streampipe).
> *"From stdin, through the pipe, into your dashboard."* Names the data path, then explains each step.

## 17 · Type Specimen

The typeface is the design. Foundry pages and design systems where a custom face is the proof.

- **Heading:** the typeface set at several sizes, demonstrating what it does.
- **Body:** a progressive demonstration: display size, body size, italic, language coverage, OpenType features.
- **Divider:** a `<figcaption>` under each specimen; a caption below is legal, a label above is an eyebrow (54).
- **Button:** one outlined action ("Buy the family") in the fold (44b), returning at the foot.
- **Image:** none; the typography is the imagery.
- **Reveal:** one type-unmask, on the first specimen as it paints; the rest is simply there.

Reach for it for type foundries, design systems where a custom face is the differentiator, font product pages.

Avoid when the brand uses an off-the-shelf face. Type Specimen needs something distinctive to celebrate.

**Sample opening lines** (foundry voice: name the face, the weights, the use):
> *"Corvid Display, set at 96pt."* Names the face and the size, nothing else.
> *"Eight weights. Three optical sizes. One good italic."* Counts the system in three short phrases.
> *"A type system for editorial."* Refusal of the verb, one noun phrase.

## 18 · Portfolio Grid

Filterable cards of projects. Studio and designer homepages where the work is the product.

- **Heading:** a short line above the grid; no display.
- **Body:** a responsive grid of project cards, same size or with slight size variation; image tracks `minmax(0, 1fr)` (50).
- **Divider:** the filter row above the grid; no internal rules.
- **Button:** a link inside each card ("View the case study"); no global CTA. The fold's one visible action is the first card's link (44b).
- **Image:** a thumbnail per card, from the user's work; until it arrives, the projects are set in type with one slot at most (68).
- **Reveal:** card fade on filter change.

Reach for it for design studios, agencies, photographer portfolios, any creative business where the work is the pitch.

Avoid for products. Portfolio Grid is a service-business shape.

Compositions: Grid with a filter row (`layout.md` § 5).

**Sample opening lines** (name the volume and the era):
> *"Selected work, 2018 to 2026."* A date range, nothing else.
> *"Twelve projects, six clients, two countries."* Three counts, no adjective.
> *"Work, indexed by year."* The index is the whole site.

## 19 · Map / Diagram

A single large spatial diagram organises the page: flowchart, floor plan, network graph, system map. Information is laid out spatially, not linearly.

- **Heading:** an orientation head at the section size above or beside the map; the map carries the page.
- **Body:** the map itself, nodes and edges, with a legend.
- **Divider:** none inside; the diagram is one composition.
- **Button:** links inside nodes; the page's one action sits with the orientation phrase, inside the fold (44b), never under the map.
- **Image:** the map is the image: SVG drawn from the real places or the real system, with hover states, labelled or `aria-hidden` with a text legend carrying every fact (33). Geometry that is geometry is a first-class medium (47c).
- **Reveal:** node-by-node ink-on as the map enters the viewport, capped at five nodes, once.

Reach for it for system overviews, ecosystem maps, process diagrams, organisation charts.

Avoid as a substitute for narrative. Some stories should not be read spatially.

Mobile: under 60rem the map scrolls sideways inside a wrapper, or collapses to an ordered list of its nodes.

**Sample opening lines** (name the path or the territory):
> *"Browser, then API, then database. Tracejam sits between the last two."* Names the layers and the position.
> *"From stdin, through the pipe, into your dashboard."* Labels the flow drawn below.
> *"Three tiers across two regions, one ledger."* Counts the system, geographic and structural.

## 20 · Ecosystem Index

Multiple discovery surfaces: featured, latest, by category, by people. The platform's value is browsing, not declaration.

- **Heading:** a prompt positioning line; no display.
- **Body:** several horizontal rails or grids, each surfacing a different cut of the platform's content.
- **Divider:** each rail opens with its own `<h2>`, never a label band; a hairline or a change of paper between rails.
- **Button:** a link at each rail's edge carrying a verb ("See all templates"); rarely a global CTA, so the fold's one visible action is the first rail's link (44b).
- **Image:** thumbnails throughout; the page is dense imagery, all of it the platform's real content.
- **Reveal:** none.

Reach for it for community platforms, content marketplaces, asset stores, any curated catalogue front page.

Avoid for single-product pages. Ecosystem needs several things to surface.

**Sample opening lines** (rail headings, dated, with a count):
> *"Featured this week."* Then *"Latest."* Then *"By category."* Three rail headings, each on its own line.
> *"What is on this week, the editor's pick, and the whole catalogue."* Names cadence, curation and breadth in one sentence.
> *"Made by the people who use it, sorted by the people who read it."* Second-position copy that breaks the template.

## 21 · Component Playground

Interactive code-and-preview blocks are the page's primary content. Each block previews a thing and shows how to copy it.

- **Heading:** each category is a real `<h2>` ("Buttons", "Forms", "Cards") in the display face, sentence case; never a label band.
- **Body:** a preview, then its code, block after block, often with a tab row to switch frameworks; the row scrolls sideways under 60rem.
- **Divider:** a change of paper per category; hairlines between examples.
- **Button:** a "Copy" button on every code block; its label swaps to "Copied", never a toast (16).
- **Image:** the previews are the imagery; one photograph band of the real machines or setting at most.
- **Reveal:** none.

Reach for it for design systems, component libraries, snippet sites, framework documentation.

Avoid for marketing pages. Playground is utility, not pitch.

Mono is legal here only inside the code blocks (64); tab labels and captions stay in the body face.

**Sample opening lines** (tangible: open on a real example, not a claim):
> *"Try it inline. Then take it home."* Two short imperatives.
> *"Every example is editable. Every output is real."* Pairs the claim with its proof.
> *"From `npm install` to your first chart in eight lines."* Names the step count, makes a concrete promise.

# Macrostructures

Twenty-one named landing-page shapes. Each is a complete fingerprint (heading placement, body composition, divider language, button voice, image treatment, reveal pattern) bundled under one name. **This is a vocabulary, not a menu.** Design the page the prompt asks for, then name the shape you designed so Rotation and gate 32 have something to read; reaching in here first and building whatever comes back is how twenty-one shapes collapse into the same three. When nothing here fits what you designed, say so, describe the shape as a fingerprint (§ The fingerprint, below), and give it a short name for the stamp and the log (*a season page*).

## The 21 macrostructures, index

**Read only the one file** for the shape you landed on, from `references/macrostructures/`. Do not load the whole catalogue. Slugs are stable; Rotation reads the shape from the stamp and the log. Nav and footer are part of the shape, settled with the hero. Each shape file names the `layout.md` compositions it is built from; the code is yours.

- **01 · Bento Grid.** Modular blocks of varying sizes laid out as an irregular grid. Each block is a feature, a figure, an image or a quote the user supplied. Rhythm comes from size variation, not card uniformity. [`macrostructures/01-bento-grid.md`](macrostructures/01-bento-grid.md)
- **02 · Long Document.** Reads like a memo, a letter or a journal entry. No marketing structure. Continuous prose with inline section heads. The page is literature about the product. [`macrostructures/02-long-document.md`](macrostructures/02-long-document.md)
- **03 · Marquee Hero.** The hero is the page above the fold. A single statement or visual fills the viewport. Below the fold the page becomes something else (a list, a grid, prose). [`macrostructures/03-marquee-hero.md`](macrostructures/03-marquee-hero.md)
- **04 · Stat-Led.** The hero is a figure the user gave, with the line that says what it means. Everything that follows supports or qualifies it. [`macrostructures/04-stat-led.md`](macrostructures/04-stat-led.md)
- **05 · Workbench.** Real product captures are the primary content. The page is a guided tour of the app in use, with short captions in place of marketing copy. [`macrostructures/05-workbench.md`](macrostructures/05-workbench.md)
- **06 · Conversational FAQ.** Bold questions, prompt answers. The page reads like an honest interview with the product. Each pair may be a disclosure. [`macrostructures/06-conversational-faq.md`](macrostructures/06-conversational-faq.md)
- **07 · Manifesto.** Polemical large type. The page tells the reader what to believe before it tells them what to buy. [`macrostructures/07-manifesto.md`](macrostructures/07-manifesto.md)
- **08 · Photographic.** A single huge image dominates each fold. Text is small annotation, not headline. The design says look before it says read. [`macrostructures/08-photographic.md`](macrostructures/08-photographic.md)
- **09 · Quote-Led.** The hero is a quote the user supplied, with its attribution. The headline is someone else's voice. [`macrostructures/09-quote-led.md`](macrostructures/09-quote-led.md)
- **10 · Specimen.** Large serif display, asymmetric spans, hairline rules, a typographic CTA, generous whitespace. Only for prompts about type, publishing or writing (a foundry, a journal, a press); the editorial genre alone does not qualify. [`macrostructures/10-specimen.md`](macrostructures/10-specimen.md)
- **11 · Catalogue.** Uniform grid of variations of the same thing: typefaces, palettes, SKUs. The page is a visual index of inventory. [`macrostructures/11-catalogue.md`](macrostructures/11-catalogue.md)
- **12 · Letter.** First-person, written, intimate. Opens with a greeting. Reads as a personal note from the founder. [`macrostructures/12-letter.md`](macrostructures/12-letter.md)
- **13 · Index-First.** The page is a list of links. No hero image, no narrative flow. Navigation as design. [`macrostructures/13-index-first.md`](macrostructures/13-index-first.md)
- **14 · Narrative Workflow.** Numbered stages tell the story of how the user uses the product over time. Each section is a phase; the page is a process timeline. [`macrostructures/14-narrative-workflow.md`](macrostructures/14-narrative-workflow.md)
- **15 · Split Studio.** Diptych. Every major block divides the screen, text on one side, proof on the other; the proof keeps its side and the rows vary by weight. [`macrostructures/15-split-studio.md`](macrostructures/15-split-studio.md)
- **16 · Feature Stack.** Sticky left pane holding the heading, scroll-synced right pane cycling through related captures. Paced like film. [`macrostructures/16-feature-stack.md`](macrostructures/16-feature-stack.md)
- **17 · Type Specimen.** The typeface is the design. Foundry pages and design systems where a custom face is the proof. [`macrostructures/17-type-specimen.md`](macrostructures/17-type-specimen.md)
- **18 · Portfolio Grid.** Filterable cards of projects. Studio and designer homepages where the work is the product. [`macrostructures/18-portfolio-grid.md`](macrostructures/18-portfolio-grid.md)

## SaaS section deck: deal it, do not sequence it

When the shape is **Bento Grid, Stat-Led, Workbench or Marquee Hero** and the prompt is a B2B SaaS page, build from this deck. Cards have roles, not positions. The base of the deck is made of things the page can show honestly without inventing anything; the top of the deck exists only when the user handed over the material.

**Base cards** (always available):

| Card | Role | Composition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spec sheet | what it is, in figures the product ships with: limits, formats, versions, regions | Table or Rows (`layout.md` § 5) |
| Worked example | the product doing one real job on the user's material: a command and its output, a capture and its caption | Showcase or Split |
| Changelog | the last three or four entries with their real dates; the page proves it is alive | Rows |
| Comparison anatomy | the product beside the way it is done today, row by row, no scores | Table |
| Pricing table | the actual price, two or three tiers; "Contact sales" on every tier says the brand does not trust the buyer | `craft.md` § 9 Pricing |
| FAQ | real objections answered like a person; "Yes, both providers work out of the box" beats "integrates with leading providers" | [`macrostructures/06-conversational-faq.md`](macrostructures/06-conversational-faq.md) |
| CTA strip | the ask, once, one button | Band |
| Footer | the close, in the theme's voice | `layout.md` § 7 |

**Material cards** (exist only when the user supplied the material, and the Picks block names what was supplied):

| Card | Needs | Without it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hero visual | a real capture | the product built in a `data-slot` (`imagery.md` § 4), or a typographic hero; never a styled-div UI outside a slot (47c) |
| Logo row | the user's own customer marks, with permission to show them | the card does not exist; no invented marks, no "Trusted by" line (46a, 54) |
| Three features | three named capabilities, each with a capture or figure to show | fold them into the worked example or the spec sheet |
| Testimonials | quotes the user supplied verbatim, with the person's name, role and company as given | the card does not exist; no plausible names, no paraphrase (46a, 19) |

**Every deal deviates twice.** (a) Drop at least one base card and name it (the CTA strip is the usual cut; footer never drops). (b) Either promote a second base card into the hero's place (a spec sheet as the hero object says "the numbers are the pitch"; a worked example as the hero says "watch it work") or reorder one adjacent pair meaningfully (pricing before the example says "the price is the pitch"). State both moves in the Picks block: `deck: -cta +changelog` or `deck: -faq · pricing<example`. A deal that keeps at least five cards still reads complete; below five it is a landing strip, not a landing page: re-add cards or switch shape.

Cards part by the three `--section-gap` steps, mixed (59), and each fills its section (`layout.md` § 4).

The deck is not a template you stamp out: the shape determines how each card looks. A Bento Grid page interleaves the spec sheet and the example inside the grid; a Stat-Led page sequences them top to bottom under the figure; a Marquee Hero page lets the marquee carry the claim and the example carry the proof.

For non-SaaS work (Editorial, Manifesto, Letter, Long Document, Quote-Led) this deck does not apply. A bakery does not need a pricing tier comparison.

## How to pick

On a theme build the draw deals the shape (SKILL.md Step 2); these steps are for a swap the material forces, or a run without Node.

0. **Read the material inventory** (SKILL.md Step 2). A shape built on screenshots or figures needs them, real or as slots the user asked for; with neither, pick a shape that carries type and facts.
1. **Read the prompt.** Note any words that strongly signal one shape ("data heavy", "tell a story", "a list of links", "many small features", "personal note").
2. **Read `.hallmark/log.json`** (newest first) and the `shape:` field of any Hallmark stamp in the project; the last three shapes are excluded.
3. **Match the prompt to a shape** using the index lines above and § Domain to trio below, then open only the file you land on. Most prompts match two to four; pick the one most distant from the logged shapes, and check the mirror test in SKILL.md Step 2.
4. **State the pick once**, in the Picks block's Shape row and the stamp's `shape:` field.
5. If torn, take the domain's trio (§ Domain to trio) and pick the one most distant from the log.

Two pages Hallmark builds for two different prompts must look like different sites, not colour swaps of one template.

## The fingerprint: six axes

**1. Heading placement.** Left-margin (marginalia beside the body; a label beside a heading is an eyebrow, gate 54) · Hanging (the heading floats above in air) · Centred display · Bottom-aligned (the heading anchors the base, content above) · Overlapping (over a photo or colour block) · Sticky or pinned · Numbered by structure (a real `<ol>` with `counter()`, or one numeral at graphic scale) · Inline with the body (no break, the heading emerges from the prose). Any placement is fair; what reads as a mistake is a narrow auto-centred head over full-width left-flush content.

**2. Body composition.** Single column · Two-column asymmetric (wide body, narrow margin for captions) · Multi-column justified with hyphenation · Marginalia (sidenotes in the outer margin) · Three equal columns (reference density) · Full-bleed with margin reset (65ch body, pull quotes and images bleed) · Asymmetric spans (2-1-3 ratios on a grid).

**3. Divider language.** Hairline rule (0.5 to 1px, inset or full-bleed) · Ornament (a fleuron, a dot, a mark) · Negative space (the gap is the divider) · Bleed-colour block (a paper change is the edge) · Double rule. Pick one language for the page and vary its weight and placement by seam (9): the same rule at the same gap at every seam is the template.

**4. Button voice.** Solid (one filled primary) · Outlined · Unstyled link (an underlined word) · Oversized solid · Typographic only (a word in a weight, no box) · Form as CTA (the action is fill-this-field).

**5. Image treatment.** Full-bleed · Tightly cropped to the grid · Inline with the text · Margin-aligned · None.

**6. Reveal pattern.** Fade-up stagger (once, orchestrated) · Horizontal sweep · Type-unmask (a clip-path opening over text) · Number-tick (counters, only on real figures) · Typewriter (a terminal only, the caret inside a typed command) · None.

Fingerprint: one choice per axis, written `Hanging|Asymmetric spans|Hairline|Outlined|Margin-aligned|None`. Two rules: coherence (choices from the same world; a justified newspaper body wants a typographic CTA, not an oversized solid) and anti-repetition (no more than three of six axes shared with any of the last three logged entries; a None on Image or Reveal that the theme or the material forces is not a shared choice).

# Microinteractions

Loaded when the page has stateful UI. `craft.md` § 5 owns the durations, the three easings and the bans; `gates.md` owns the tells (10, 11, 12, 15, 16, 17, 18, 26, 27, 62); the theme's Motion section decides how much moves. This file owns the recipes, and repeats none of them.

## Principles

- **Motion has a job or it is cut.** Every animation clarifies, guides or confirms. Ask what would be lost if it were instant; if nothing, remove it.
- **Silent success.** When the user can see the result, no toast. Toasts are for failures and for effects the page cannot show.
- **Optimism with rollback.** Update the interface at once, send the request behind it, and roll back with a way to retry when it fails.
- **Reduced motion is a state, not an afterthought.** Every recipe below names it: spatial motion collapses to a 150ms opacity crossfade, functional state still changes.
- **Keyboard first.** Every hover affordance has a focus equivalent; nothing is hover-only.
- **Three primitives at most per page** (a reveal, a hover signal, one functional loop such as a marquee or a counter count as three). A theme whose character is still runs none beyond functional state changes.

## Recipes

Durations are `--dur-micro` 120ms, `--dur-short` 220ms and `--dur-long` 420ms; enters `--ease-out`, exits `--ease-in` at 60 to 75% of the enter, toggles `--ease-in-out`. A spring appears only under a declared spring posture on a playful theme, on the primary control and one character moment (12).

**Button press.** Hover is one signal, a colour change; press is a 1px drop, released on pointer up. The focus ring never animates.

```css
.btn { transition: background-color var(--dur-short) var(--ease-out), transform var(--dur-micro) var(--ease-out); }
.btn:hover { background: var(--color-paper-3); }
.btn:active { transform: translateY(1px); }
```

**Input focus.** The outline appears at once, inset on inputs; the border may deepen one step but its width never changes (39a). The label sits above the field at rest and never moves: a floating label starts life as a placeholder, which is the tell.

**Validation.** First on blur once the field has been touched, then on every input; never on the first keystroke. The helper line swaps for the error in the same reserved line (F14): what broke, why, what to do. `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` on the field.

**Toast.** Failures and invisible effects only (16). One corner, newest pushes the stack one way, nothing else repositions. In over `--dur-long`, 4 to 6s dwell, out at 65%; auto-dismiss pauses on hover and focus; an error toast carries one retry action and does not leave on its own.

**Modal.** A `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`, `inert` on the page behind it. Backdrop fades and the panel scales 0.96 to 1 over `--dur-long` `--ease-out`; it closes at about 65% with `--ease-in`. First focus goes to the first interactive element, not the close button. Reduced motion: the 150ms crossfade.

**Menu.** The Popover API (light-dismiss, Escape and stacking for free), CSS anchor positioning that flips within 16px of an edge. Opens over `--dur-short` `--ease-out`, closes at 65% with `--ease-in`; items may stagger 30ms when there are eight or fewer.

**Tooltip.** Hover delay 800 to 1000ms, focus delay 0 (17); opacity over `--dur-micro`. It stays while the pointer moves onto it and leaves on Escape (WCAG 1.4.13).

**Tab change.** The indicator moves by `transform` (translate and scale on the x axis, never `width`) over `--dur-short`; the outgoing panel fades at `--dur-micro`, the incoming one follows. A panel that changes height animates `grid-template-rows: 0fr` to `1fr`, never `height`.

**Number tick.** Real figures only (46a). On data load, count from the previous value (zero on first load) over 400 to 800ms with `--ease-out` applied to the value, formatted by `Intl.NumberFormat`. Announce only the final value (`aria-live="polite"`). Reduced motion: the final value at once.

**Copy to clipboard.** The label swaps to *Copied* for 2.5s; no toast, the label is the feedback.

```js
btn.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  await navigator.clipboard.writeText(value);
  btn.dataset.state = "copied";
  setTimeout(() => delete btn.dataset.state, 2500);
});
```

**Drag to reorder.** The handle appears on hover and on focus; the cursor is `grab`, then `grabbing`; a ghost at 50% opacity follows the pointer and a 1px accent line marks the drop target. Release snaps over `--dur-short` `--ease-out`, no spring. Arrow keys reorder a focused row; `aria-live` announces the move.

**Optimistic update.** The row changes at once and the request runs behind it. Success says nothing. Failure rolls the row back over `--dur-short` and raises a toast with *Try again*, which stays until acted on.

```js
const prev = item.done;
item.done = !prev; render();
try { await api.update(item); }
catch { item.done = prev; render(); toast({ tone: "error", message: "Could not save.", action: { label: "Try again", run: retry } }); }
```

**Search as you type.** Debounce 250ms; while waiting, a quiet signal on the field (the border one step deeper). Matches in `<mark>`. Announce the result count once the debounce settles, never per keystroke.

**Command palette.** Opens at once on ⌘K or `/`; the input keeps focus throughout. Arrow keys move a highlight that slides by `transform` over `--dur-micro`; the rows themselves never move. Enter selects, Escape closes. Rows may fade in on first open, never on filtering.

**Page-load reveal.** One orchestrated entrance, per `craft.md` § 5: staggered by DOM order, 0.4 to 0.8s in all, IntersectionObserver rather than scroll listeners, once. A still theme skips it, and that is correct.

## Motion character

Every system declares one: a catalog theme in its Motion section, a custom page in its own stylesheet. The same press is louder in a severe system than in a calm one.

| Character | Duration scale | Feels like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **still** | none | Print. Nothing moves; a caret may blink inside a typed command, four or five beats and then solid, never on its own. |
| **severe** | 0.7 to 0.75 times | Fast and decisive; snaps into place; no spring anywhere. |
| **brisk** | 0.85 to 0.9 times | Technical and functional: an instrument panel. |
| **calm** | 1.0 to 1.3 times | Restrained to generous, `--ease-out` at its gentlest. |

Most pages have too much motion, not too little. The static answer is usually the right one.

# Redesign

Loaded only when the user names Hallmark with `redesign` or `audit` (`/hallmark redesign <target>`, *redesign the site with Hallmark*). A request that changes an existing design without naming Hallmark (a restyle, new colours or a new theme, a polish, a redesign, a small edit) never loads this file: it is done as asked, in the project's own system. A redesign is a build whose material is the page that exists: SKILL.md still binds, and this file says what the run keeps, what replaces the Step 1 ask and what the sweep adds. The target is the user's own code (a file, a folder, a route on a dev server); a live URL with no source behind it can only be audited, through `--url`.

## What a redesign keeps

- **The content.** Every fact, claim, name, price, date and quote the page states. Figures, quotes and logos already there are the user's material: carried over as found and listed in the handoff to verify, one a gate doubts (a trend nobody measured, 46a) included. Nothing is added: no action, section, claim or picture the page did not have, beyond what the user hands over and what a gate requires (a pause on a loop, 18; a focus ring). A drawing made from the page's own facts (its channels, its steps, a figure) is composition, and full depth may make one.
- **The wiring.** Every link, form, field, handler, route, id and test hook; every script, data call and analytics call. Edit markup inside the component that owns it. Never move logic, rename a prop, or drop a `name`, an `id`, a `key`, a `type`, an `href` or a `data-testid` that a script or a test reads. A prop the Floor empties (an emoji passed as an icon) may go with it, named in the handoff. A state the screen has no logic for (a failed load, an undo) is listed for the owner, never built.
- **The files.** No file deleted, no route removed and no component tree replaced without a file-level plan the user approved, and no test edited to make the redesign pass. Documents in the repo (a README, a prompt, a deck) explain the product; they are not page copy. In a git project, start from a clean tree, `.hallmark/` aside (ask the user to commit or stash; never do it for them), so the redesign is one diff they can read and revert. The stylesheet is the redesign's to edit: the append-only rule guards it from a build, not from its own redesign.
- **The brand,** when there is one. A brand is chosen: a logo, a colour or a face the project names (a brand file, a logo asset, named tokens, a font file of its own) or the user states. It stays at every depth, its values read from the project's files, never from memory. A framework default or a look the gates name (the purple-to-blue gradient, Inter as the display, a stock swatch) is not a brand: restyle and full replace it, and the Picks block says so in case it was. A locked `design.md` is the system at every depth.
- **The words,** unless a gate names them. Wording that fails a copy gate (19, 54, 58, 63, 69) is tightened from the facts already on the page, and the handoff lists every changed line, before and after. An eyebrow is never just deleted: where its heading is figurative, the plain label becomes the heading (*Opening hours* over *When to find us* becomes *Opening hours*). Terms, disclaimers and consent text are never reworded. When the user says to keep every word, stamp `copy: verbatim`: 19, 58 and 69 then report as notes.

## Depth

The verb is a **full** redesign: the content and the wiring stay, the system and the composition change. A lighter depth runs only when the same request asks for it in so many words, and the Picks block names the depth:

| Depth | Stays | Changes | Only when the request says |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **full** | the content and the wiring | the system and the composition: shape, hero, section objects, chrome | nothing else: it is the verb |
| **restyle** | the layout | the system: colour, type, radius, shadow, motion, the controls | *keep the layout*, *restyle*, *reskin*, *only the colours and type* |
| **polish** | the system and the layout | only what a gate names: the tells, contrast, states, motion, tokens | *polish*, *keep our look*, *only fix what looks generated* |

The depths do not blend: a polish that finds the concept wrong says so and recommends the full run, it never smuggles one in.

**Full depth on an app screen** recomposes each screen inside the shell it has: what leads, and how the figures, tables and forms are arranged (`flow.md` § App screens). Routes, destinations and each component's logic stay; there is no hero stage and no hero review.

*From scratch* is a build, not a depth: SKILL.md as written, the old page as its Step 2 inventory, in new files beside the old ones.

## Before

1. Run the pre-flight (Step 0), then list the pages in the target: route, file, and whether each is a page or an app screen (`flow.md` § App screens). In a framework project start the dev server and record through `--url`; the linter does not render the empty shell `index.html` from disk. An unstamped page has no genre: infer it from the page as Step 1 would from a prompt, and say so.
2. Record the page as it stands:

```
node <skill-dir>/scripts/sloplint.mjs <target> --genre <genre> --render --before [--url <route> ...] [--scope app]
```

It prints the findings grouped by gate and writes them to `.hallmark/before.txt`, the screenshots to `.hallmark/before/` and the record to `.hallmark/before.json`: every link, form, field, inline handler, test hook, script tag, selector a script queries, heading and figure. Git ignores the folder's screenshots and records.

3. Look at the screenshots before you weigh the findings, so the linter does not write the verdict, then give the read in four lines: what the page is for (the audience, the one action); what works and stays (at least one thing); what reads as generated (the worst tells, by gate); what is broken.

**`audit <target>` stops here.** It loads `gates.md` § 1, § 4 and § 5, walks the judged gates from the screenshots, and reports the findings by tier with `file:line`, the read, the lightest depth that settles them and what only a deeper one would. It changes none of the project's files.

## The ask

One message replaces the Step 1 ask; skip it when the request already answers it or no one can answer:

> *Before I redesign, three things. 1. **What must stay**: the brand, a section, a page? Say *keep the layout* and I only restyle. 2. **What is wrong with it**, in your words, and the feeling you want instead. 3. **Anything new to show**: screenshots, photos, numbers, a quote. Or say **go ahead** and I will redesign it in full.*

## The plan

The Picks block opens with four rows of its own, and nothing is deleted until the user has seen the Files row:

```markdown
- **Redesign** · full · 3 pages (/, /pricing, /docs)
- **Before** · Floor 14 FAIL · Reflex 9 · a centred template in a stock indigo; the pricing table is clear and stays
- **Keeps** · every link, field and handler · the green and the brand face · the pricing table
- **Files** · edit: app/page.tsx, app/pricing/page.tsx, app/globals.css · create: app/tokens.css, app/base.css · delete: none
```

Then the build rows the depth reaches: Theme at restyle and full (dealt, `brand` or locked); Shape, Chrome, Hero, Signature and Sections at full only, where Step 2 runs with the page's own content as its inventory. At polish the block stops after Files. The deal's `--prompt` is the read's first line (what the page is for, in plain nouns), never the page's own copy, which is what the redesign is leaving behind.

## Build

- **Polish** is `flow.md` § The sweep, on the user's own page: fix in place, single elements and tokens, never restructure, under the check stamp with `built: the project · redesign: polish`. It loads `gates.md` § 1 to § 5 and `patterns.md`, `interaction-and-states.md` when the page has a form, the theme file an old stamp names, and from `craft.md` only the section a finding points at.
- **Where the layout stays** (polish and restyle), the stamp's `redesign:` field tells sloplint to report the layout gates (6b, 8, 9, 32, 42, 44a, 44c, 58, 77, 79) as notes; at polish the spacing and scale gates (24b, 59, 78) too, so a polish does not re-space a site it was asked to keep. Print them for the user with the depth that would settle them; do not rebuild them. At every depth 58 (the screen budget) is a note too: the words are the owner's, and only a copy gate cuts one. In app scope those gates are skipped, so the handoff's Layout row comes from the read and the review. A theme's own composition rules (its do-nots, the dials that vary between pages) yield to a kept layout: the theme lends its system, and every page takes one dial set.
- **Restyle and full** start from the scaffold, with the depth in the stamp: `theme.mjs scaffold <slug> --redesign <depth>`, or `scaffold --brand --redesign <depth>` for a kept brand, its tokens filled from the palette and faces the pre-flight found (no `check`: the coordinates are the user's); add `--scope app` for app screens. It writes `tokens.css` and `base.css` beside the project's stylesheet and prints the imports that fit it (`export-formats.md` has the Tailwind and shadcn names). Then the shared components and the chrome, then the pages, the most visited first, each swept before the next.
- **More than one page** at restyle or full: lock the system once the scaffold has run (`design-md.md`). Every page reads it and the variety rule inverts: pages share theme, type and accent, and differ only in shape. One stylesheet for several pages lists a hero posture per route, `hero: Settled (/), Stage (/contact)`. Past three pages, give each page to its own subagent where the harness has them, with `design.md`, the page's files and this file.
- **Full depth** runs the hero stage and the hero review; polish and restyle skip both. The old sections still sit below the new hero at that stage: the stage judges the first screen alone, and what it reports below the fold waits for the sweep. Gate 8 judges the composition, not the order of the content: a kept sequence in a new composition is waived on the record.

## After

1. The sweep, against the record: `sloplint <target> --genre <genre> --render --kept`. Anything the page had and no longer has is a `FAIL kept` (a link, a form, a field, a handler, a test hook, a script, a selector a script still queries) or a `WARN kept` (a heading, a figure, an image, an id). Restore it, or put it on the record in the stamp: `/* Hallmark · dropped /blog, #team · the user is retiring the blog and the team section */`, or for a line a copy gate named, `/* Hallmark · reworded "Built for modern teams" to "Out of your way" · 19 names the opener */`, or `dropped "<the line>" · 69 names it` for a line a gate cuts whole. The run also writes `.hallmark/compare.html`, the before and after screenshots side by side: give the user its path.
2. The project's own checks, where it has them: the type check, the build, the tests. A redesign that breaks one is not finished.
3. The finish review also takes the `before` screenshots and answers what the old page did better (`review-finish.md`). A polish hands it only the full pages at 1440, before and after, and takes at most five findings. A finding that is a plain defect (a misalignment, a broken glyph, a label that lies) is fixed at any depth; one that asks for a new composition joins the layout findings; one that asks for content the page never had goes to the owner in the handoff.
4. The log entry carries `mode: redesign`, `depth` and `scope` (page, site or app), plus the build's fields at full depth.
5. The handoff, ahead of the material ask; where the layout stayed it adds a Layout row (the findings only a full redesign would settle):

```

Before   Floor 14 FAIL · Reflex 9
After    Floor 0 · Reflex 1 waived (47b)
```
